notes: Short post-judgment order on costs and ancillary matters following Saint-Gobain patent appeal; limited substantive issues.

enrichment.short_title: Saint-Gobain v Fusion Provida: Court of Appeal costs and ancillary orders
key_facts: Following the Court of Appeal's dismissal of Fusion Provida's obviousness appeal in the Saint-Gobain buried-pipe patent case, the court was asked to resolve residual matters.
The successful respondent sought all costs of the appeal including those of its respondent's notice.
The appellants sought interest on costs before Pumfrey J, a certificate of contested validity and permission to appeal to the House of Lords.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Supplemental Court of Appeal hearing on costs and ancillary orders after the main patent appeal judgment.
enrichment.outcome: The respondent was awarded all costs of the appeal including the respondent's notice; no summary assessment was made in the Court of Appeal; interest on Court of Appeal costs was ordered at the judgment rate; no order was made for interest on Pumfrey J's costs; no certificate of contested validity was granted; and permission to appeal was refused as a matter for the House of Lords.
enrichment.ratio: A proper respondent's notice may attract full costs even if unsuccessful; post-judgment costs interest and certificates of contested validity are matters for the trial judge or House of Lords rather than the Court of Appeal on a supplemental hearing.
legal_issues: Whether costs of a respondent's notice should be included in the appeal costs order
Whether the Court of Appeal should summarily assess costs or order interest on first-instance costs
Whether a certificate of contested validity should be granted on appeal
Whether the Court of Appeal should grant permission to appeal to the House of Lords
linked_authorities: Saint-Gobain PAM SA v Fusion Provida Ltd [2005] EWCA Civ 177

notes: Drink-driving mouth-alcohol appeal; Crown Court evidential reasoning and Quick Test admissibility upheld.

enrichment.short_title: O'Sullivan v DPP: mouth alcohol and breath specimen reliability
key_facts: The appellant was convicted of driving with excess alcohol after evidential breath readings of 71 and 73 micrograms.
Controlled tests showed the Intoximeter could not reliably detect mouth alcohol, raising an issue whether the specimens were affected by regurgitation.
The Crown Court relied on the positive roadside test, closeness of the two readings, a later Quick Test result and the appellant's weak medical evidence.
The appellant had indigestion and heartburn history but gave no evidence of regurgitation at the material time.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from the Crown Court dismissal of an appeal against conviction for excess alcohol.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the Crown Court was entitled to be sure the specimens were not affected by mouth alcohol and lawfully admitted the Quick Test evidence to rebut the regurgitation suggestion.
enrichment.ratio: Where mouth alcohol is alleged, the fact-finder may rely on the totality of evidence including roadside test results, closely matching evidential readings and subsequent Quick Test results; a Quick Test used only to rebut mouth alcohol is not an impermissible substitute for the statutory evidential procedure.
legal_issues: Whether reliance on the roadside breath test was Wednesbury unreasonable
Whether closeness of two evidential readings excluded mouth alcohol without expert reasons
Whether Quick Test results were admissible despite lack of calibration and statutory procedure
Whether the Crown Court unfairly treated the appellant's inability to recall regurgitation

notes: Major patent obviousness appeal; Jacob LJ's Johnsson and obvious-to-try analysis is authoritative.

enrichment.short_title: Saint-Gobain v Fusion Provida: buried pipe patent obviousness upheld
key_facts: Saint-Gobain's patent claimed zinc-aluminium alloy coating with a porous pore-sealing layer for buried cast-iron pipes.
Fusion Provida argued claim 1 was obvious over the Johnsson paper published just before the priority date.
The skilled person sought long-term corrosion protection by white rust formation and healing at coating defects, which Johnsson did not address.
Pumfrey J held the patent valid; the Court of Appeal applied the Biogen deference principle to obviousness.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Pumfrey J's judgment holding European Patent (UK) No 0686246 valid and infringed on an obviousness challenge only.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; claim 1 was not obvious because Johnsson gave no pointer that Zn/Al alloy would provide the critical corrosion-product protection needed for buried pipes.
enrichment.ratio: Substituting Zn/Al alloy for Zn in black pipe was not an obvious step where the prior art was silent on white rust formation and defect healing; 'obvious to try' requires a sufficient likelihood of success, not mere inclusion in a research programme.
legal_issues: Whether Johnsson made Zn/Al substitution for buried pipes obvious
Whether historical non-adoption of the substitution was a relevant factor
Whether the judge erred by relying on historical considerations given Johnsson's date
Application of the Biogen principle to appellate review of obviousness
linked_authorities: Biogen Inc v Medeva plc [1997] RPC 1
Windsurfing International Inc v Tabur Marine (Great Britain) Ltd [1985] RPC 59
Johns-Manville Corporation's Patent [1967] RPC 479

notes: Landmark TCC penalty clause judgment; Jackson J's four-issue analysis on Onslow House LADs is comprehensive.

enrichment.short_title: McAlpine v Tilebox: liquidated damages clause not a penalty
key_facts: McAlpine contracted to refurbish Onslow House, Guildford, for Tilebox under a JCT contract with LADs of £45,000 per week.
Tilebox had funding obligations under a DFA with Standard Life requiring timely completion.
The parties negotiated the LAD rate as a pre-estimate based on minimum rental value during pre-contract discussions.
McAlpine sought a declaration that clause 24.2 was an unenforceable penalty after substantial delay.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Part 8 claim in the Technology and Construction Court for a declaration that a liquidated damages clause was a penalty.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; clause 24.2 was a reasonable pre-estimate of foreseeable losses including DCP erosion, Tilebox's direct costs and back-to-back liability to Standard Life.
enrichment.ratio: A substantial discrepancy, not mere excess at the top of the range, is required before a commercial liquidated damages clause will be struck down; courts are predisposed to uphold freely negotiated LAD provisions where parties of comparable bargaining power debated the figure.
legal_issues: Whether clause 6.8.2 of the DFA required completion by a specific date
Whether clause 6.8.1 imposed back-to-back completion liability to Standard Life
What losses from delay were foreseeable on contract date
Whether £45,000 per week was an extravagant penalty or genuine pre-estimate

Commissioner of Public Works v Hills [1906] AC 368
Philips Hong Kong Ltd v Attorney General of Hong Kong [1993] 61 BLR 41

notes: Attorney General's Reference on unduly lenient racially aggravated GBH sentences; clear uplift guidance.

enrichment.short_title: AG Reference: unduly lenient sentences for racially aggravated GBH
key_facts: Three offenders pleaded guilty to racially aggravated grievous bodily harm after attacking two Turkish men following an England-Turkey football match.
Onaranoglu suffered a fractured skull requiring a titanium plate and lost his restaurant partnership.
The group attack involved racial abuse, kicking and stamping on a defenceless victim.
The Crown Court sentenced each offender to two years' imprisonment for the GBH offence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's Reference on the ground that sentences for racially aggravated grievous bodily harm were unduly lenient.
enrichment.outcome: Reference allowed; substituted sentences of three years for Broad and Matthews and three years plus a consecutive twelve months for Sellars, reflecting an eighteen-month uplift for the racial aggravation with double-jeopardy reduction.
enrichment.ratio: Racially aggravated assault occasioning or inflicting grievous bodily harm warrants a substantial sentencing uplift for deterrence; where the judge failed to reflect the racial element, an increase of about eighteen months may be appropriate depending on the circumstances.
legal_issues: Whether two-year sentences adequately reflected racial aggravation
What uplift is appropriate under Saunders for racially aggravated GBH
Whether guilty pleas and lack of prior serious violence limited the uplift
Application of double jeopardy reduction on an Attorney General's Reference
linked_authorities: R v Saunders [2000] 1 Cr App R 458
R v Moore (1992) 13 Cr App R (S) 130
R v Jane [1998] 2 Cr App R (S) 363

notes: VAT input tax limitation appeal; Collins J disapplies three-year cap for accrued rights but dismisses on delay.

enrichment.short_title: Fleming v HMRC: VAT input tax time limit and accrued rights
key_facts: Bodycraft purchased thirteen Aston Martin cars in 1989-90 and recovered input VAT on ten cars in 1994 but held no VAT invoices.
Regulation 29(1A) from May 1997 imposed a three-year cap on input tax repayment claims without transitional provisions.
The appellant's 2000 claim for input tax on the three remaining cars was refused for breach of the three-year limit.
The tribunal accepted Marks & Spencer principles prevented reliance on the cap but dismissed on discretion grounds.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal under section 11(1) of the 1992 Act from the VAT and Duties Tribunal refusal of input tax repayment.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; although accrued rights could require disapplication of the cap, the appellant's delay of over three years after the limitation took effect meant the claim was rightly refused; related judicial review proceedings were also dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: Directly effective Community law rights to VAT repayment may require disapplication of a retroactive limitation period lacking transitional protection, but disapplication is not indefinite and a claimant who waits years after the cap takes effect cannot rely on accrued rights to recover input tax.
legal_issues: Whether regulation 29(1A) could be disapplied for pre-1997 accrued input tax rights
Whether the October 2000 claim was part of the earlier 1993 claim
Whether lack of transitional provisions rendered the cap unlawful under Marks & Spencer
Whether delay after the cap took effect defeated the claim despite disapplication

notes: Corporate libel damages ruling; Gray J strikes out reliance on unsued follow-up articles.

enrichment.short_title: Collins Stewart v Financial Times: corporate libel and follow-up publications
key_facts: Collins Stewart sued over a Financial Times article of 27 August 2003 repeating serious allegations from a former analyst's FSA report.
The newspaper published further articles on 28 and 30 August 2003 but these were not sued as separate libels.
Collins Stewart sought to rely on the follow-up articles to increase damages for the original publication.
The Financial Times applied to strike out paragraph 8.3 of the Particulars of Claim on the basis that corporations cannot recover aggravated damages.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory application to strike out particulars seeking to rely on subsequent publications to increase damages in a corporate libel claim.
enrichment.outcome: Paragraph 8.3 struck out; a corporate claimant may not increase compensatory damages for a single sued publication by relying on subsequent unsued articles, and aggravated damages for injury to feelings are unavailable to companies.
enrichment.ratio: Aggravated damages in libel compensate injury to feelings, which a corporation cannot suffer; subsequent publications that could have been separate causes of action should generally be sued separately rather than used to inflate damages for an earlier libel.
legal_issues: Whether follow-up publications may increase damages for an original libel
Whether corporations may recover aggravated or exacerbation damages
Whether an apology reducing damages has a converse aggravated-damages counterpart for companies
Whether the strike-out application was barred by delay or overreaching
linked_authorities: Broome v Cassell & Co Ltd [1972] AC 1027
Rookes v Barnard [1964] AC 1129
Lewis v Daily Telegraph Ltd [1964] AC 234

notes: Long Chancery judgment on MTIC VAT fraud and freezing-order variation applications; three interveners refused.

enrichment.short_title: Regalway Care v Shillingford: freezing order and MTIC fraud interveners
key_facts: Regalway Care, in liquidation, obtained a freezing order against defendants including EBST in suspected MTIC VAT carousel fraud.
Three interveners applied to vary the order so EBST could repay them about £1.35 million for mobile phones and computer chips.
The liquidator questioned whether the transactions were genuine or knowing participation in missing-trader intra-Community fraud.
Evidence showed rapid same-day chains, fixed mark-ups, lack of security and uncertainty over whether goods reached their destination.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Applications by third-party interveners to vary a freezing order in Chancery proceedings arising from suspected MTIC fraud.
enrichment.outcome: Applications refused without summary disposal; the judge was not satisfied on the evidence that EBST should be permitted to make the payments, and directed separate trials of the intervener claims.
enrichment.ratio: Where serious doubt exists whether payments from a frozen defendant to trade creditors reflect genuine transactions or knowing involvement in MTIC fraud, a court should not vary a freezing order to permit large irrecoverable payments without full investigation, disclosure and cross-examination.
legal_issues: Whether interveners showed good arguable claims justifying release of frozen funds
Whether the transactions were genuine commercial deals or MTIC carousel fraud
Whether 21st Century Logistic Solutions Ltd v Madysen applied where fraud knowledge was disputed
How the intervener claims should be case-managed for trial

notes: Asylum out-of-time permission appeal; merits must be addressed even where only remittal is sought.

enrichment.short_title: Secretary of State v Makke: out-of-time asylum appeal and merits requirement
key_facts: Sudanese national Makke claimed asylum but did not attend the adjudicator hearing because London and Newcastle solicitors failed to communicate.
The adjudicator determined the appeal in absentia and dismissed it on the merits.
The respondent applied out of time to the IAT for permission to appeal seeking only remittal for a fresh hearing.
Wilson J quashed the IAT refusal; the Court of Appeal restored it.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Secretary of State's appeal against a High Court decision quashing the Immigration Appeal Tribunal's refusal of out-of-time permission to appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; permission to appeal out of time was rightly refused because the respondent never addressed whether the adjudicator's decision was wrong on the merits.
enrichment.ratio: An applicant for out-of-time permission to appeal must show a real prospect of success on the merits, not merely loss of a hearing; procedural unfairness does not justify extension where the applicant declines to identify arguable errors in the underlying asylum decision.
legal_issues: Whether loss of a hearing alone suffices for out-of-time permission
Whether failure to address merits in the permission application was fatal
Whether the respondent's personal lack of fault required grant of permission
Application of Simeer and Nazarina to consistent IAA decision-making
linked_authorities: Simeer v Immigration Appeal Tribunal [2003] EWHC Admin 2683
Ko Ko Naing v Immigration Appeal Tribunal [2003] EWHC Admin 771

notes: Shelltime 4 Hague-Visby time-bar ruling; Cresswell J follows Stena Pacifica on cargo claims.

enrichment.short_title: Borgship Tankers v Product Transport: Shelltime 4 cargo time bar
key_facts: Charterers sub-chartered the tanker Casco on Shelltime 4 after carrying palm oil cargoes.
Sahara cancelled a gasoline sub-charter because tank cleaning left the vessel unsuitable to load the nominated cargo.
Charterers claimed about US$795,000 for lost sub-charter freight and wasted bunkers due to alleged uncargoworthiness.
Owners contended the claims were time-barred under clause 27(c)(ii) incorporating the Hague-Visby one-year limit.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court preliminary issue in arbitration on whether charterers' claims were time-barred under Shelltime 4 clause 27(c)(ii).
enrichment.outcome: Claims held not time-barred; the loss-of-use claim for cancelled sub-charter freight was not a cargo claim within clause 27(c)(ii) and was not measured by reference to cargo, following The Stena Pacifica.
enrichment.ratio: Clause 27(c)(ii) of Shelltime 4 applies only to cargo claims of the kind normally brought by cargo interests for loss or damage relating to and measured by reference to cargo; a charterer's claim for loss of employment after cancellation of a sub-charter is independent of the Hague-Visby Rules time bar.
legal_issues: Whether the freight claim arose out of loss or damage in connection with cargo
Whether Article III rule 6 applied to uncargoworthiness causing sub-charter cancellation
Whether charter breaches were co-extensive with or independent of Hague-Visby obligations
Whether The Stena Pacifica governed clause 27(c)(ii) construction
